title: 200% Rule Strategy
name: 200% Rule Strategy
metaTitle: 200% Rule Strategy in San Diego, CA
metaDescription: 200% rule identification strategy for San Diego investors who need more than three real candidates in a supply-constrained market, without padding the list.

sections.html: The 200% rule lets a San Diego investor identify any number of replacement properties on the 45-day letter, as long as the combined fair market value of everything listed does not exceed twice the value of the property sold. It exists for exactly the situation San Diego investors run into constantly: a market too tight to bank an exchange on three candidates when half of them may not survive due diligence.

sections.heading: Why the Three-Property Rule Falls Short Here
sections.html: The default three-property rule works fine in markets with deep, liquid inventory. It works less well when your relinquished property funds a purchase in Sorrento Valley lab space or Torrey Pines-adjacent office-lab, where listings are thin and a seller can pull a deal off the table with a phone call. Investors who limit themselves to three names on the identification letter are often betting the entire exchange on properties they have not fully underwritten yet.

sections.heading: A Real List Versus a Padded One
sections.html: Here is where a lot of quotes for "identification strategy" get thin: some providers will happily list eight or ten properties to stay under the 200% ceiling without ever pressure-testing whether any of them could actually close. A padded list satisfies the paperwork and does nothing else. We run each candidate through the same basic filter, lender feasibility, seller motivation, and title condition, before it goes on your letter, so every name is a property you could actually buy, not a placeholder.

sections.heading: Running the Math Before You Sign
sections.html: The 200% ceiling is calculated on fair market value at the time of identification, not asking price, and it applies to the sum of every property on the letter, not each one individually. Adding a fourth or fifth candidate late can push the total over the ceiling without anyone noticing until it is too late to fix. We recalculate the running total every time a property is added or a valuation changes, so the letter you sign is accurate the day it goes to the qualified intermediary.

sections.heading: What Actually Belongs on the Letter
sections.html:
A workable San Diego identification letter under the 200% rule usually mixes property types across a few submarkets rather than stacking similar risk in one corridor. Candidates worth including typically share:

  • A seller who has confirmed willingness to negotiate on timeline
  • Financing that a lender has pre-screened, not only quoted
  • Title that has already been pulled and reviewed
  • A price within the exchange's basis and boot targets

sections.heading: What Happens If the List Gets Challenged
sections.html: If the fair market value of the full list is later shown to exceed 200% and you did not close on at least 95% of the value identified, the entire identification can be disqualified. That is a real risk in a market where valuations move between the 45-day letter and closing. Confirm any valuation dispute or late addition to the letter with your qualified intermediary and tax advisor before treating a padded list as a safe fallback.

sections.heading: Why a Cheap Identification Package Can Cost More Later
sections.html:
Some providers price identification strategy as a flat, low fee precisely because the work involved is minimal, fill in names, confirm the ceiling math, send the letter. That version of the service protects the paperwork, not the exchange. If two of the three candidates on a bare-bones letter turn out to be unfinanceable in week six, the investor is back to square one with far less runway than they started with.

We price the work around the actual screening, seller confirmation, lender pre-check, and title review, because that is what determines whether an identification letter is a real safety net or a document that merely exists. Ask what specifically was checked on each candidate before it went on your list, beyond whether the math on the 200% ceiling adds up.

A useful gut check is asking how many of the listed candidates the provider could actually describe in detail without pulling up notes, current asking terms, seller circumstances, financing feasibility. A list assembled from a quick database search tends to produce vague answers, while a genuinely screened list produces specifics on each name.

faqs.q: Can I identify more than three properties on a San Diego exchange?
faqs.a: Yes, under the 200% rule, as long as the combined fair market value of every property listed does not exceed twice the sale price of the relinquished property.

faqs.q: Does adding more names to the list lower my risk?
faqs.a: Only if each name is a property you could realistically close on. A long list of unvetted candidates satisfies the rule on paper but does not protect you if none of them are financeable or available.

faqs.q: What happens if my identified properties add up to more than 200%?
faqs.a: The identification can be disqualified unless you close on at least 95% of the total value listed. This is why we recalculate the running total every time a property is added.

faqs.q: Is the 200% rule based on asking price or fair market value?
faqs.a: Fair market value at the time of identification, which is why valuations need to be checked, not assumed from a listing price, especially in a market like San Diego where prices move quickly.

faqs.q: Should I use the 200% rule instead of the three-property rule by default?
faqs.a: Not automatically. It makes sense when San Diego's thin inventory in a given asset class makes three candidates too risky. In deeper submarkets, three well-vetted properties can be simpler to manage.
